newsitem.title: RUSSIA: OSCE to monitor Chechen poll if safety permits.
newsitem.headline: OSCE to monitor Chechen poll if safety permits.

text.p: Preparations are being made for at least 50 foreign observers to monitor post-war elections in Chechnya if it is safe in the rebel region, an OSCE official said on Wednesday.

Tim Guldimann, who heads the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe's mission in Chechnya, said the murder of six foreign Red Cross workers there last month made him fear further assassinations.

But he said a recent spate of violence in Chechnya, which included the shooting of a group of Russians, had eased and he hoped it would remain calm until the January 27 election, called after a 21-month war between Moscow and separatists.

"I have the impression...that the terrorist actions in December, or at least part of those actions, were aimed at creating conditions to make the elections difficult," Guldimann told a news conference at Interfax news agency in Moscow.
"I was very afraid that it would continue, and the fact that it has stopped up to now is a good sign that maybe the arrests which were made will help to bring about relative stability."

Chechnya's separatist authorities say they have arrested gunmen suspected of shooting the six Red Cross workers, five of them women, as they lay in their beds in a hospital compound in the Chechen village of Novye Atagi on December 17.
Thierry Meyrat, head of the Moscow delegation of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), said on Wednesday his colleagues, who left Chechnya after the murders, were still deeply shaken.
"A decision on the renewal of the ICRC's activities in Chechnya depends directly on the discovery of who committed the crime, its reasons and motives," Interfax quoted him as saying.

Moscow says it has withdrawn all troops sent to Chechnya two years ago to stop it splitting from Russia. The Russian forces were humiliated in 21 months of fighting which killed tens of thousands of people, mainly civilians.
Russian officals have backed the January 27 elections, even though the main candidates insist on Chechen independence, and have aproved the idea of sending foreign observers.
Guldimann said a final decision on the presence of observers would be made by the OSCE's permanent council on January 16.
"The preparation concerns 50 to 70 observers under the auspices of the OSCE, but it hasn't been decided yet," he said.

Controversy over the vote has already begun. The Chechens have gone back on an agreement with Moscow to conduct voting in regions outside Chechnya where tens of thousands of refugees, many of them Russian, are now living.

Guldimann said refugees would be able to vote on Chechnya's borders and that a failure to hold voting elsewhere would not invalidate the ballot. Russian officials were not immediately availiable for comment.
He said he hoped that prisoners of war on both sides would be amnestied after the vote.
Moscow says more than 1,000 Russian troops are missing. The Chechen military command said on Tuesday 1,380 Chechens had been reported missing.
